title: Five minutes and a plate of beans
lead: Organizers have named the judges for a robot hand contest in Japan. Teams will use chopsticks or tweezers to move roasted beans one at a time.

news.title: Can a robot hand move beans with chopsticks?
news.summary: Organizers in Japan picked judges for a contest in which robot hands will move roasted beans one at a time. Teams can use chopsticks or tweezers and will have five minutes.
news.details: Organizers in Japan picked five judges for a robotic hand contest.
news.technical_novelty: Each hand will move roasted beans from one plate to another, one bean at a time, with chopsticks or tweezers.
news.engineering_impact: A team can control the hand from a distance or teach a program to do the job beforehand.
news.limitations: Applications close December 18. The final is still ahead.
news.evidence_status: The contest organizers published the rules and judges.
news.organization: GMO Internet Group, GMO AIR and Singularity Society
news.body:
Five judges have been named for a contest in Japan where a robot hand will move roasted beans between plates. The organizers from GMO will give each team five minutes. The hand has to pick up one bean at a time with chopsticks or tweezers. The judges will look at speed and accuracy.

Imagine trying to lift one bean with chopsticks. If the sticks slip in your hand, their tips can come apart. If the tips hold the bean too loosely, it can fall. A person can control the robot's fingers from a distance or train a program to carry out the movements beforehand.

Applications close December 18, and the final is planned for March 26 in Tokyo. Teams can try equipment at a lab before the event. That gives them time to check how their hand grips a tool and what happens when a bean rolls on the plate.

news.title: The robot loaded the machine, then walked over for the part
news.summary: Bigwave Robotics tested a two-legged robot at a South Korean factory. It loaded an engine part, walked to the other station and set the finished part on a cart.
news.details: At a factory in South Korea, a robot loaded an engine part into a machine and walked to the place where finished parts come out.
news.technical_novelty: The robot and the machine exchanged signals so each could start at the right moment.
news.engineering_impact: The trial shows how one robot can do several jobs at two places on a line.
news.limitations: The company reported a test and gave no count for a full shift.
news.evidence_status: Bigwave Robotics, which prepared the robot for the task, described the trial.
news.body:
At a South Korean factory, a robot put an engine part into a machine that straightens it. After that machine did its work, the robot walked about ten metres to the place where finished parts come out. It put the processed part on a cart. Bigwave Robotics was testing whether one robot could do all of that on an existing line.

Timing matters for both machines. If the robot comes for a part too soon, there is nothing ready to pick up. The equipment and the robot exchanged signals, a bit like a teammate telling you they have finished their part of a job. The signals tied together work going on in two different places.

The robot got practice at walking inside a computer simulation. It learned how to grab parts from examples of the movement. Then the company tried the sequence at a real factory. The announcement did not say how often it could repeat the whole trip during a work shift.

news.title: The box looks empty. What if it is heavy?
news.summary: Yunbei Zhang and colleagues tested what happens when a robot inside a computer tries to move an object that gets heavier. Their program watches how the arm moved and uses that clue to adjust the next command.
news.details: Researchers tested how to correct a robot’s motion when its arm became weaker or an object got heavier in a computer simulation.
news.technical_novelty: The software checks how far the arm moved and adjusts the next command.
news.engineering_impact: That gives the robot another way to carry out the same plan.
news.limitations: The tests used a robot inside a computer.
news.evidence_status: Yunbei Zhang and colleagues described the experiment and its results.
news.organization: Tulane University, New York University, Nanyang Technological University, MIT and Harvard University
news.body:
Researchers led by Yunbei Zhang tested a robot inside a computer. They changed the weight of objects or how strongly its arm could move. They wanted to see if a program could notice the arm had moved less than intended and correct the next instruction.

Think of two identical cardboard boxes. One is empty and one is full of books. Until you try to lift them, they look the same. When the robot's arm moved less than expected, that gave its program a clue. The program used the clue to decide whether to adjust the next movement or leave the command alone.

In one set of computer tests with changed conditions, about 28 attempts out of 100 worked before the adjustment and about 63 worked with it. The researchers measured those results in a simulation. They did not test whether a physical robot could use the same clue to lift a real box.

news.title: Helping a computer get through a big calculation
news.summary: Amazon agreed to buy software technology that helps computer chips work more efficiently. Those chips can help developers train programs that control robots.
news.details: Amazon agreed to buy technology that can help chips carry out large numbers of calculations more efficiently.
news.technical_novelty: The software changes how calculations are carried out on different chips.
news.engineering_impact: That can help computers train programs and run the ones they have already trained.
news.limitations: The agreement still needs approval. Amazon gave no figure for how much faster programs would run after the purchase.
news.evidence_status: Amazon announced the agreement. Reuters reported that the company declined to disclose the price.
news.body:
Amazon agreed to buy technology from a company called Decart. It helps a computer carry out many calculations on a chip. For example, people can use calculations like these when they show a program many examples of a robot arm moving and train it to choose what to do next.

Imagine a group of friends working on different parts of a big problem. If one person needs another’s answer right away, they may have to wait. Computers also split a big calculation into smaller pieces. This software helps choose an order that works well for the chip doing the work.

The two companies have worked together on Amazon’s chips since 2025. Amazon announced the agreement on November 23, and the deal still needs approval. Amazon has not said how much time it would save someone trying to train a program for their own robot.

news.title: How do you tell if the pan went to the wrong place?
news.summary: Researchers at the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence tried a robot in a kitchen inside a computer. When the arm left a pan in the wrong place, software told it to move the pan onto the right burner.
news.details: Researchers tested whether a robot can spot a mistake before moving on to its next job.
news.technical_novelty: One part of the software controls movement. Another checks what happened.
news.engineering_impact: If an object is in the wrong place, the program can give the robot a new instruction to put it right.
news.limitations: The result comes from a kitchen inside a computer.
news.evidence_status: Researchers showed an example of a correction in their paper.
news.body:
A team at the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence tested a robot in a kitchen inside a computer. One of its jobs involved a pan. The team wanted to see if checking after a movement would help when the robot managed to lift the pan but set it down in the wrong place.

Suppose you have to put a pan on the left burner and then put a spoon away. You want to check that the pan is in place before moving on to the spoon. In the test, one part of the software controlled the arm. Another checked the result and could ask for a new movement.

Across the computer kitchen’s tasks, about 60 attempts out of a hundred worked without that extra check and about 65 worked with it. The paper shows one example where the robot moved a pan again to get it right. The team wants to find out how the program deals with surprises in other places and with other robots.

technology_signal.title: One challenge for different robot hands
technology_signal.summary: The GMO organizers set a five-minute limit for moving roasted beans. A person can control the hand from a distance or train a program to move it.
technology_signal.implications: If the hand loses its grip on a chopstick, the tips can separate and the bean can fall. Teams have time to test their designs before the final in Tokyo.
